Providing evidence for this hypothesis would enable researchers to exploit universal properties, facilitating the generalization of mechanistic interpretability techniques across models. Previous works studied if LLMs learned the same features, which are internal representations that activate on specific concepts. Since comparing features across LLMs is challenging due to polysemanticity, in which LLM neurons often correspond to multiple unrelated features rather than to distinct concepts, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been employed to disentangle LLM neurons into SAE features corresponding to distinct concepts. In this paper, we introduce a new variation of the universality hypothesis called Analogous Feature Universality: we hypothesize that even if SAEs across different models learn different feature representations, the spaces spanned by SAE features are similar, such that one SAE space is similar to another SAE space under rotation-invariant transformations. Evidence for this hypothesis would imply that interpretability techniques related to latent spaces, such as steering vectors, may be transferred across models via certain transformations. To investigate this hypothesis, we first pair SAE features across different models via activation correlation, and then measure spatial relation similarities between paired features via representational similarity measures, which transform spaces into representations that reveal hidden relational similarities. Our experiments demonstrate high similarities for SAE feature spaces across various LLMs, providing evidence for feature space universality.

papers.title: Enhancing Multimodal Large Language Models Complex Reason via Similarity Computation
papers.research_question: How can the complex reasoning ability of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) be improved by efficiently utilizing image information and filtering out irrelevant image tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that image tokens semantically related to text have information flow convergence and higher attention scores in the LLM decoder, and proposes Simignore, a method to filter irrelevant image tokens based on similarity computation, which improves complex reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Simignore method, which computes similarity between image and text embeddings to filter irrelevant tokens, enhances the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Image tokens semantically related to text prompts are more likely to have information flow convergence and receive higher attention scores in the LLM decoder.
Filtering out irrelevant image tokens based on similarity between image and text embeddings improves the accuracy of LVLMs on complex reasoning tasks.
The performance improvement depends on the number of tokens ignored, with an optimal number (e.g., 124 out of 576 for LLaVA1.5-7B) yielding the best results.
Important image tokens (with high similarity to text) are crucial for complex reasoning, while unimportant tokens can be ignored to improve performance and reduce computation.
Cosine similarity performs better than Euclidean and Manhattan distance for computing the similarity between image and text embeddings in this task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not adaptively choose the number of image tokens to ignore.
The internal mechanisms of how image and textual information work together to facilitate complex reasoning are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring strategies for adaptively choosing the number of image tokens to ignore.
Investigating the internal mechanisms of the model to more fully understand how image and textual information work together.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have experienced rapid growth, and numerous different models have emerged. The interpretability of LVLMs remains an under-explored area. Especially when faced with more complex tasks such as chain-of-thought reasoning, its internal mechanisms still resemble a black box that is difficult to decipher. By studying the interaction and information flow between images and text, we noticed that in models such as LLaVA1.5, image tokens that are semantically related to text are more likely to have information flow convergence in the LLM decoding layer, and these image tokens receive higher attention scores. However, those image tokens that are less relevant to the text do not have information flow convergence, and they only get very small attention scores. To efficiently utilize the image information, we propose a new image token reduction method, Simignore, which aims to improve the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs by computing the similarity between image and text embeddings and ignoring image tokens that are irrelevant and unimportant to the text. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for complex reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Transformers trained on proteins can learn to attend to Euclidean distance
papers.research_question: How can standard Transformers learn to measure Euclidean distance and function as structure models for 3D data, such as proteins?
papers.core_contribution: Standard Transformers can learn to measure Euclidean distance and function as structure models when given linear embeddings of coordinates, without requiring architectural modifications.
papers.conclusion: Standard Transformers are capable of structural reasoning by learning SE(3)-invariant distance filters, providing a basis for using them as hybrid structure-language models for proteins and other 3D tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can learn to approximate a 3D Gaussian attention filter of relative distance when given linear embeddings of coordinates.
Transformers need at least n+2 embedding dimensions to learn distance in R^n.
Data augmentation with random rotations improves SE(3)-invariance and reduces overfitting.
Adding coordinates to a protein Transformer improves masked token prediction and sequence recovery, especially for amino acids with distinct backbone conformations.
Pretraining a protein Transformer with coordinates and then finetuning for function prediction outperforms custom structural models like DeepFRI.
future_direction: Applying the method to other domains like small molecules, 3D objects, vision Transformers, and large language models.
papers.abstract: While conventional Transformers generally operate on sequence data, they can be used in conjunction with structure models, typically SE(3)-invariant or equivariant graph neural networks (GNNs), for 3D applications such as protein structure modelling. These hybrids typically involve either (1) preprocessing/tokenizing structural features as input for Transformers or (2) taking Transformer embeddings and processing them within a structural representation. However, there is evidence that Transformers can learn to process structural information on their own, such as the AlphaFold3 structural diffusion model. In this work we show that Transformers can function independently as structure models when passed linear embeddings of coordinates. We first provide a theoretical explanation for how Transformers can learn to filter attention as a 3D Gaussian with learned variance. We then validate this theory using both simulated 3D points and in the context of masked token prediction for proteins. Finally, we show that pre-training protein Transformer encoders with structure improves performance on a downstream task, yielding better performance than custom structural models. Together, this work provides a basis for using standard Transformers as hybrid structure-language models.

papers.title: DeepFRI Demystified: Interpretability vs. Accuracy in AI Protein Function Prediction
papers.research_question: How interpretable and robust is the DeepFRI model for protein function prediction, and how do different explainability methods compare in highlighting influential residues?
papers.core_contribution: The study reveals that DeepFRI's predictions prioritize conserved structural motifs over functional residues, and different explainability methods offer varying levels of granularity, highlighting trade-offs between accuracy and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: DeepFRI has strengths in conserved domains but limitations in complex proteins, and interpretability methods must be chosen carefully to balance robustness and precision for biological insights.
papers.key_findings:
DeepFRI's predictions often prioritize structural motifs like beta sheets over functional residues, leading to potential misinterpretations.
GradCAM provides broad heatmaps with low sparsity, Excitation Backpropagation offers binary masks with high sparsity, and PGExplainer gives precise per-residue scores.
The model is robust to mutations, requiring over 200 mutations in some cases to cause misclassification, but this may overlook biologically significant changes.
Sparsity analysis shows that explainability methods vary significantly, with GradCAM being the least sparse and Excitation Backpropagation the most sparse.
Using an ensemble of explainability methods can highlight high-confidence residues and areas of epistemic uncertainty.
papers.limitation:
DeepFRI prioritizes structural motifs over functional residues, potentially leading to inaccurate interpretations of protein function.
The model's robustness to mutations may cause it to overlook biologically significant changes unless a large fraction of the structure is disrupted.
DeepFRI's message-passing can overlook long-range or allosteric effects in complex regulatory proteins.
future_direction: Guide experimental validation through targeted mutagenesis based on explainability results.
Fuse GCN topology with per-residue embeddings from protein language models for improved sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Machine learning technologies for protein function prediction are black box models. Despite their potential to identify key drug targets with high accuracy and accelerate therapy development, the adoption of these methods depends on verifying their findings. This study evaluates DeepFRI, a leading Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) based tool, using advanced explainability techniques (GradCAM, Excitation Backpropagation, and PGExplainer) and adversarial robustness tests. Our findings reveal that the model's predictions often prioritize conserved motifs over truly deterministic residues, complicating the identification of functional sites. Quantitative analyses show that explainability methods differ significantly in granularity, with GradCAM providing broad relevance and PGExplainer pinpointing specific active sites. These results highlight tradeoffs between accuracy and interpretability, suggesting areas for improvement in DeepFRI's architecture to enhance its trustworthiness in drug discovery and regulatory settings.

papers.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders for Monosemantic Representation
papers.research_question: How do concept activation distributions differ between Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and their base models, and do SAEs promote more monosemantic representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a distribution-aware concept separability score and shows that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) reduce polysemanticity and achieve higher concept separability than their dense base models. It also proposes a new intervention method, Attenuation via Posterior Probabilities (APP), which enables effective concept removal with minimal side effects.
papers.conclusion: This work presents the first quantitative analysis of monosemanticity in SAEs compared to dense base models through a distributional lens, introduces a fine-grained concept separability score, and proposes a new intervention method (APP) that achieves effective concept removal with the least possible side effects.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs exhibit lower polysemanticity (neuron overlap) and higher concept separability than their base models across multiple datasets and models.
SAEs enable more precise concept-level interventions than base models, particularly when using partial suppression methods.
The proposed APP intervention method achieves the smallest perplexity increase while remaining highly competitive at concept removal.
Higher-capacity SAEs (e.g., 65k dimensions) yield greater concept separability and more effective interventions than lower-capacity ones.
A strong positive correlation exists between the concept separability score and the precision of partial concept erasure methods.
papers.limitation: APP uses a histogram-based approximation for density estimation to improve computational efficiency, which trades off accuracy and computational cost. Achieving the best possible performance requires significantly higher computational resources.
future_direction: Future work could explore alternative kernel density estimation (KDE) methods to better balance accuracy and efficiency for the APP method.
papers.abstract: A key barrier to interpreting large language models is polysemanticity, where neurons activate for multiple unrelated concepts. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed to mitigate this issue by transforming dense activations into sparse, more interpretable features. While prior work suggests that SAEs promote monosemanticity, no quantitative comparison has examined how concept activation distributions differ between SAEs and their base models. This paper provides the first systematic evaluation of SAEs against base models through activation distribution lens. We introduce a fine-grained concept separability score based on the Jensen-Shannon distance, which captures how distinctly a neuron's activation distributions vary across concepts. Using two large language models (Gemma-2-2B and DeepSeek-R1) and multiple SAE variants across five datasets (including word-level and sentence-level), we show that SAEs reduce polysemanticity and achieve higher concept separability. To assess practical utility, we evaluate concept-level interventions using two strategies: full neuron masking and partial suppression. We find that, compared to base models, SAEs enable more precise concept-level control when using partial suppression. Building on this, we propose Attenuation via Posterior Probabilities (APP), a new intervention method that uses concept-conditioned activation distributions for targeted suppression. APP achieves the smallest perplexity increase while remaining highly effective at concept removal.

papers.title: An Empirical Study of Memorization in NLP
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether the long-tail theory of memorization holds in NLP, specifically whether memorized training instances are atypical and whether memorizing them helps generalization, and proposes a method to attribute memorization to input features.
papers.core_contribution: The paper empirically validates the long-tail theory of memorization in NLP, showing that memorized instances are atypical and their removal harms generalization, and introduces a memorization attribution method to identify which input features are memorized.
papers.conclusion: The paper validates the long-tail theory in NLP, showing memorization is important for generalization, and the attribution method helps understand memorization behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Top-ranked memorized training instances are likely atypical.
Removing top-memorized training instances leads to a more serious drop in test accuracy compared to removing random instances.
The proposed memorization attribution method is faithful and can identify tokens that require memorization.
The top-memorized parts of a training instance tend to be features negatively correlated with the class label.
papers.limitation:
Computation of influence functions is massive due to inverting hessian matrices.
Memorization increases vulnerability to privacy attacks, creating a trade-off between accuracy and privacy.
future_direction: Adopt hessian-free influence estimators like TracIn to reduce computation costs.
papers.abstract: A recent study by Feldman (2020) proposed a long-tail theory to explain the memorization behavior of deep learning models. However, memorization has not been empirically verified in the context of NLP, a gap addressed by this work. In this paper, we use three different NLP tasks to check if the long-tail theory holds. Our experiments demonstrate that top-ranked memorized training instances are likely atypical, and removing the top-memorized training instances leads to a more serious drop in test accuracy compared with removing training instances randomly. Furthermore, we develop an attribution method to better understand why a training instance is memorized. We empirically show that our memorization attribution method is faithful and share our interesting finding that the top-memorized parts of a training instance tend to be features negatively correlated with the class label.

papers.title: Too Big to Think: Capacity, Memorization, and Generalization in Pre-Trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does model capacity affect the trade-off between memorization and generalization in pre-trained Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Small Transformer models generalize to unseen arithmetic cases but fail to memorize facts, while larger models memorize facts but fail to extrapolate; no model size achieves both when tasks are combined, indicating an inherent trade-off between memorization and generalization.
papers.conclusion: The trade-off between memorization and generalization is a structural consequence of model capacity, not just a byproduct of training dynamics. Future language model design should account for this trade-off, possibly via modular architectures that separate memorization from generalization pathways.
papers.key_findings:
The smallest model (n14) achieves perfect accuracy on held-out arithmetic cases but only 8.2% on factual recall.
Larger models (n28, n56, MLT) achieve perfect factual recall but fail on all held-out arithmetic cases.
Intermediate models show a transition from generalization to memorization as capacity increases.
When trained jointly on both tasks, no model generalizes to held-out arithmetic cases, and the smallest model's performance degrades on both tasks.
Extended training (1.5M iterations) on the arithmetic task for the large model did not lead to generalization (no grokking observed).
papers.limitation: The n14 model's generalization is shallow and does not extend to multi-digit inputs, indicating limited extrapolation rather than robust generalization.
future_direction: Explore whether these dynamics extend to real-world domains.
Investigate training strategies to better balance memorization and generalization.
Explore modular or specialized architectures that separate memorization from generalization pathways.
papers.abstract: The relationship between memorization and generalization in large language models (LLMs) remains an open area of research, with growing evidence that the two are deeply intertwined. In this work, we investigate this relationship by pre-training a series of capacity-limited Transformer models from scratch on two synthetic character-level tasks designed to separately probe generalization (via arithmetic extrapolation) and memorization (via factual recall). We observe a consistent trade-off: small models extrapolate to unseen arithmetic cases but fail to memorize facts, while larger models memorize but fail to extrapolate. An intermediate-capacity model exhibits a similar shift toward memorization. When trained on both tasks jointly, no model (regardless of size) succeeds at extrapolation. These findings suggest that pre-training may intrinsically favor one learning mode over the other. By isolating these dynamics in a controlled setting, our study offers insight into how model capacity shapes learning behavior and offers broader implications for the design and deployment of small language models.

papers.title: SAEs Are Good for Steering -- If You Select the Right Features
papers.research_question: How to distinguish between input and output features in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to improve the effectiveness of steering language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a taxonomy of SAE features into input and output types, introduces input and output scores to identify them, and demonstrates that selecting features with high output scores significantly improves steering performance, making unsupervised SAE steering competitive with supervised methods.
papers.conclusion: The work formalizes the roles of SAE features, provides practical scores for feature selection, and shows that output features are key to effective steering, bridging the gap between unsupervised and supervised steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Features in SAEs can be categorized as input features, which capture input patterns, or output features, which influence model outputs.
High input and output scores rarely co-occur in the same features, with input features common in early layers and output features in later layers.
Features with high output scores are more effective for coherent and high-quality steering compared to those with high input scores.
Filtering SAE features based on output scores leads to 2-3x improvements in steering performance on benchmarks like AxBench.
With proper feature selection, SAE steering achieves performance close to supervised methods such as LoRA.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is restricted to features extracted from the residual stream, and does not account for features derived from other components such as attention or MLP layers.
Method focuses on steering using a single SAE feature, ignoring interactions between features that may lead to better effects.
future_direction: Understanding how multiple features combine or interfere for better steering effects.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed as an unsupervised approach to learn a decomposition of a model's latent space. This enables useful applications such as steering - influencing the output of a model towards a desired concept - without requiring labeled data. Current methods identify SAE features to steer by analyzing the input tokens that activate them. However, recent work has highlighted that activations alone do not fully describe the effect of a feature on the model's output. In this work, we draw a distinction between two types of features: input features, which mainly capture patterns in the model's input, and output features, which have a human-understandable effect on the model's output. We propose input and output scores to characterize and locate these types of features, and show that high values for both scores rarely co-occur in the same features. These findings have practical implications: after filtering out features with low output scores, we obtain 2-3x improvements when steering with SAEs, making them competitive with supervised methods.

papers.title: Efficient Dictionary Learning with Switch Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we scale sparse autoencoders efficiently to reduce compute cost while maintaining performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Switch Sparse Autoencoders, a novel SAE architecture that uses a mixture-of-experts style routing to reduce compute cost and memory bottlenecks while maintaining reconstruction performance and feature interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Switch SAEs are a promising approach for scaling sparse autoencoders, providing a Pareto improvement in FLOPs vs. MSE without significant reduction in feature interpretability, and may enable large-scale SAE training on GPU clusters.
papers.key_findings:
Switch SAEs achieve better reconstruction than dense TopK SAEs at a fixed compute budget (FLOP-matched).
Switch SAEs require more total features (parameters) to achieve the same reconstruction as dense SAEs when trained to convergence, but this gap narrows for larger SAEs.
In FLOP-matched settings, Switch SAEs Pareto-dominate TopK, Gated, and ReLU SAEs in terms of reconstruction MSE and fraction of loss recovered.
Switch SAEs exhibit feature duplication across experts, which reduces capacity, but this effect diminishes at larger sparsities.
Switch SAE features are as interpretable as TopK SAE features in FLOP-matched settings, and in width-matched settings they have higher true positive rates but lower true negative rates in automated interpretability detection.
papers.limitation:
Switch SAEs have reduced performance at a fixed number of parameters compared to dense SAEs, especially for attention and MLP layers.
Only the simplest mixture-of-experts architecture is investigated, leaving open the question of maximum performance gain from more sophisticated MoE architectures.
No downstream evaluations of Switch SAEs (e.g., feature steering or circuit discovery) are conducted.
future_direction: Investigate feature deduplication techniques, more sophisticated routing architectures, and multiple active experts.
Explore more sophisticated mixture-of-experts architectures like GShard, DeepSeekMoE, and expert choice routing.
Conduct downstream evaluations of Switch SAEs, such as feature steering or circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a recent technique for decomposing neural network activations into human-interpretable features. However, in order for SAEs to identify all features represented in frontier models, it will be necessary to scale them up to very high width, posing a computational challenge. In this work, we introduce Switch Sparse Autoencoders, a novel SAE architecture aimed at reducing the compute cost of training SAEs. Inspired by sparse mixture of experts models, Switch SAEs route activation vectors between smaller "expert" SAEs, enabling SAEs to efficiently scale to many more features. We present experiments comparing Switch SAEs with other SAE architectures, and find that Switch SAEs deliver a substantial Pareto improvement in the reconstruction vs. sparsity frontier for a given fixed training compute budget. We also study the geometry of features across experts, analyze features duplicated across experts, and verify that Switch SAE features are as interpretable as features found by other SAE architectures.

papers.title: Group-SAE: Efficient Training of Sparse Autoencoders for Large Language Models via Layer Groups
papers.research_question: How can the computational cost of training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for LLMs be reduced while maintaining performance? Specifically, can grouping similar layers and training a single SAE per group achieve this?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Group-SAE, a method to reduce the computational cost of training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for LLMs by grouping layers with similar residual stream representations and training a single SAE per group, guided by a novel metric called AMAD (Average Maximum Angular Distance).
papers.conclusion: Group-SAE provides an efficient and scalable strategy for training SAEs in modern LLMs, achieving significant computational savings without compromising reconstruction quality, downstream task performance, or interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Group-SAE reduces the number of SAEs needed, cutting training costs by up to 50% with minimal impact on reconstruction quality and downstream performance.
The proposed AMAD metric effectively guides the selection of an optimal number of layer groups, balancing efficiency and performance.
Group-SAEs achieve comparable or slightly better interpretability scores (Detection and Fuzzing) than baseline per-layer SAEs.
Features learned by a Group-SAE are most similar to the baseline SAE trained on a layer within its group, and individual features typically peak at a specific layer but spread to adjacent ones.
The method outperforms alternative efficiency baselines like training smaller SAEs on all layers or using evenly spaced groups, especially on downstream performance metrics.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models from the Pythia family trained on the Pile dataset, and the generality to other architectures (e.g., Gemma, LLaMA) or datasets is not evaluated.
The study uses a fixed expansion factor (c=16) and TopK activation function; the impact of these hyperparameter choices is not investigated.
The interpretability evaluation is limited due to the high cost of annotating large numbers of features; a more comprehensive analysis is needed.
future_direction: Further optimizing the number of layer groups and scaling the approach to even larger models.
Evaluating the method on additional datasets and across diverse model architectures (e.g., Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral).
Conducting a more comprehensive and systematic interpretability analysis.
papers.abstract: Sparse AutoEncoders (SAEs) have recently been employed as a promising unsupervised approach for understanding the representations of layers of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, with the growth in model size and complexity, training SAEs is computationally intensive, as typically one SAE is trained for each model layer. To address such limitation, we propose Group-SAE, a novel strategy to train SAEs. Our method considers the similarity of the residual stream representations between contiguous layers to group similar layers and train a single SAE per group. To balance the trade-off between efficiency and performance, we further introduce AMAD (Average Maximum Angular Distance), an empirical metric that guides the selection of an optimal number of groups based on representational similarity across layers. Experiments on models from the Pythia family show that our approach significantly accelerates training with minimal impact on reconstruction quality and comparable downstream task performance and interpretability over baseline SAEs trained layer by layer. This method provides an efficient and scalable strategy for training SAEs in modern LLMs.

papers.title: Interpretability as Compression: Reconsidering SAE Explanations of Neural Activations with MDL-SAEs
papers.research_question: How can we use the Minimal Description Length principle to train and select Sparse Autoencoders that provide concise and interpretable explanations of neural activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an information-theoretic framework that views SAEs as lossy compression algorithms for neural activations, using the Minimal Description Length principle to select SAEs that provide concise and interpretable explanations, and introduces the property of independent additivity for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the MDL principle provides a theoretical motivation for SAE architectures and hyperparameters, and can help in creating principled evaluations for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs can be viewed as communication protocols for transmitting neural activations, and the MDL principle can be used to select SAEs that balance accuracy and conciseness.
Interpretability requires independent additivity, meaning features should be understandable separately.
On MNIST, MDL-SAEs find stroke-like features that are more interpretable and composable than features from very sparse or dense SAEs.
Optimizing for MDL can reduce undesirable feature splitting compared to optimizing for sparsity alone.
Hierarchical feature structures can lead to more efficient coding schemes and lower description length.
papers.limitation: The MDL principle is treated as a strategy for model selection: to choose a model out of a collection of multiple models. However, training multiple models with a hyperparameter sweep may be computationally expensive.
future_direction: Future work could look to include the entropy term in the loss function and optimise for it directly through either a straight-thought estimation approach or with a Bayesian prior.

Future work could explore to what extent variants in SAE architectures can decrease the MDL of communicated latent feature activations, and exploiting causal structure inherent in the data distribution may be important to efficient coding.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a useful tool for interpreting the internal representations of neural networks. However, naively optimising SAEs for reconstruction loss and sparsity results in a preference for SAEs that are extremely wide and sparse. We present an information-theoretic framework for interpreting SAEs as lossy compression algorithms for communicating explanations of neural activations. We appeal to the Minimal Description Length (MDL) principle to motivate explanations of activations which are both accurate and concise. We further argue that interpretable SAEs require an additional property, "independent additivity": features should be able to be understood separately. We demonstrate an example of applying our MDL-inspired framework by training SAEs on MNIST handwritten digits and find that SAE features representing significant line segments are optimal, as opposed to SAEs with features for memorised digits from the dataset or small digit fragments. We argue that using MDL rather than sparsity may avoid potential pitfalls with naively maximising sparsity such as undesirable feature splitting and that this framework naturally suggests new hierarchical SAE architectures which provide more concise explanations.

papers.title: FaithfulSAE: Towards Capturing Faithful Features with Sparse Autoencoders without External Dataset Dependencies
papers.research_question: How does training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on out-of-distribution data affect their stability and feature faithfulness, and can training on the model's own synthetic data improve these aspects?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes FaithfulSAE, a method to train Sparse Autoencoders on the model's own synthetic data, which improves feature stability and reduces fake features compared to training on external datasets.
papers.conclusion: Training SAEs on the model's own synthetic data (FaithfulSAE) improves feature consistency and reduces fake features, advancing interpretability by better capturing model-internal features.
papers.key_findings:
FaithfulSAEs trained on synthetic data show higher stability across seeds compared to SAEs trained on instruction datasets.
FaithfulSAEs achieve lower Fake Feature Ratio in 5 out of 7 models compared to web-based dataset trained SAEs.
FaithfulSAEs outperform web-based SAEs in SAE probing tasks, indicating better reconstruction of the model's hidden state.
Shared Feature Ratio is higher when the target model and source model for synthetic data are the same, indicating that SAE training on its own data is more stable.
papers.limitation:
Lack of evaluation on instruction-tuned or reasoning models.
Shared Feature Ratio may not fully reflect the complexity of high-dimensional feature spaces.
Did not assess the interpretability of individual features through case studies.
future_direction: Exploring improved dataset generation and training strategies that could completely outperform Web-based methods.
Evaluating whether Faithful SAEs provide meaningful and interpretable explanations for individual features through detailed case studies.
Investigating the connection between pruning Fake Features and the principle of Minimal Description Length.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising solution for decomposing large language model representations into interpretable features. However, Paulo and Belrose (2025) have highlighted instability across different initialization seeds, and Heap et al. (2025) have pointed out that SAEs may not capture model-internal features. These problems likely stem from training SAEs on external datasets - either collected from the Web or generated by another model - which may contain out-of-distribution (OOD) data beyond the model's generalisation capabilities. This can result in hallucinated SAE features, which we term "Fake Features", that misrepresent the model's internal activations. To address these issues, we propose FaithfulSAE, a method that trains SAEs on the model's own synthetic dataset. Using FaithfulSAEs, we demonstrate that training SAEs on less-OOD instruction datasets results in SAEs being more stable across seeds. Notably, FaithfulSAEs outperform SAEs trained on web-based datasets in the SAE probing task and exhibit a lower Fake Feature Ratio in 5 out of 7 models. Overall, our approach eliminates the dependency on external datasets, advancing interpretability by better capturing model-internal features while highlighting the often neglected importance of SAE training datasets.

papers.title: Decoding Dark Matter: Specialized Sparse Autoencoders for Interpreting Rare Concepts in Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently capture rare, subdomain-specific concepts in foundation models using sparse autoencoders, without simply scaling the SAE width?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Specialized Sparse Autoencoders (SSAEs) for capturing rare, subdomain-specific concepts in foundation models, and demonstrates their effectiveness in capturing tail concepts and improving bias mitigation.
papers.conclusion: SSAEs provide a powerful new lens for interpreting foundation models in subdomains, effectively capturing rare concepts and offering practical utility in tasks such as bias mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
SSAEs capture a greater proportion of tail concepts than standard SAEs trained on general-purpose data.
Dense retrieval is an effective data selection strategy for training SSAEs, outperforming sparse retrieval (BM25).
Tilted Empirical Risk Minimization (TERM) improves concept recall in SAEs, especially for rare concepts, at the cost of some precision.
In a case study on the Bias in Bios dataset, SSAEs achieve a 12.5% increase in worst-group classification accuracy when used to remove spurious gender information.
TERM-trained SAEs exhibit stronger activations and lower entropy for tail concepts, making them suitable for rare concept detection.
papers.limitation:
SSAEs require a small seed concept dataset to begin the data selection process.
TERM prioritizes recall, sacrificing some control (precision) for broader concept coverage.
future_direction: Extending SSAEs to other domains and modalities
Applying SSAEs to real-world safety-critical systems
papers.abstract: Understanding and mitigating the potential risks associated with foundation models (FMs) hinges on developing effective interpretability methods. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising tool for disentangling FM representations, but they struggle to capture rare, yet crucial concepts in the data. We introduce Specialized Sparse Autoencoders (SSAEs), designed to illuminate these elusive dark matter features by focusing on specific subdomains. We present a practical recipe for training SSAEs, demonstrating the efficacy of dense retrieval for data selection and the benefits of Tilted Empirical Risk Minimization as a training objective to improve concept recall. Our evaluation of SSAEs on standard metrics, such as downstream perplexity and $L_0$ sparsity, show that they effectively capture subdomain tail concepts, exceeding the capabilities of general-purpose SAEs. We showcase the practical utility of SSAEs in a case study on the Bias in Bios dataset, where SSAEs achieve a 12.5\% increase in worst-group classification accuracy when applied to remove spurious gender information. SSAEs provide a powerful new lens for peering into the inner workings of FMs in subdomains.

papers.title: Learning Multi-Level Features with Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we train sparse autoencoders to learn hierarchical features and avoid pathologies like feature absorption and splitting when scaling dictionary size?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders, a hierarchical variant that trains multiple nested dictionaries simultaneously to learn features at different levels of abstraction, reducing feature absorption and splitting.
papers.conclusion: Matryoshka SAEs are a superior alternative for practical interpretability tasks, enabling training of arbitrarily large SAEs while retaining interpretable features at different levels of abstraction.
papers.key_findings:
Matryoshka SAEs significantly reduce feature absorption and splitting compared to standard SAEs.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve more disentangled latent representations and better performance on sparse probing and targeted concept erasure tasks.
Matryoshka SAEs maintain or improve downstream task performance with increasing dictionary size, unlike standard SAEs which often degrade.
Matryoshka SAEs exhibit a small trade-off in reconstruction fidelity but learn more meaningful features that result in comparable downstream model loss.
The hierarchical structure forces early latents to capture general concepts and later latents to specialize, preserving interpretable features at multiple scales.
papers.limitation:
Slightly reduced reconstruction performance compared to standard SAEs.
Increased training time due to multiple nested reconstruction objectives.
Reliance on quantitative metrics that may not fully capture human-relevant interpretability.
future_direction: Investigate the human interpretability of Matryoshka SAE latents.
Explore the applicability of Matryoshka SAEs to practical interpretability tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for interpreting neural networks by extracting the concepts represented in their activations. However, choosing the size of the SAE dictionary (i.e. number of learned concepts) creates a tension: as dictionary size increases to capture more relevant concepts, sparsity incentivizes features to be split or absorbed into more specific features, leaving high-level features missing or warped. We introduce Matryoshka SAEs, a novel variant that addresses these issues by simultaneously training multiple nested dictionaries of increasing size, forcing the smaller dictionaries to independently reconstruct the inputs without using the larger dictionaries. This organizes features hierarchically - the smaller dictionaries learn general concepts, while the larger dictionaries learn more specific concepts, without incentive to absorb the high-level features. We train Matryoshka SAEs on Gemma-2-2B and TinyStories and find superior performance on sparse probing and targeted concept erasure tasks, more disentangled concept representations, and reduced feature absorption. While there is a minor tradeoff with reconstruction performance, we believe Matryoshka SAEs are a superior alternative for practical tasks, as they enable training arbitrarily large SAEs while retaining interpretable features at different levels of abstraction.

papers.title: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for "Quirky" Language Models
papers.research_question: Can internal model features be used to detect anomalous training signals (when models use faulty heuristics) in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Mechanistic anomaly detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks but are not effective across all models and tasks; MAD may be effective in low-stakes applications but requires advances for high-stakes settings.
papers.conclusion: Anomaly detection results are inconsistent across models and tasks; while sometimes highly discriminative, performance degrades to chance in some cases, indicating that more work is needed for reliable real-world application.
papers.key_findings:
Anomaly detector performance varies significantly between models (model-dependent detection).
Detection efficacy is strongly task-dependent (e.g., arithmetic tasks yield higher performance).
Larger deviations in behavior generally make anomalies easier to detect, though not universally.
Anomaly detection performance is closely related to the linear separability of features between normal and anomalous classes.
Detectors that depend on different features (activations vs. attribution) offer somewhat independent signals, but naive combination did not improve performance.
papers.limitation: The manipulations in the datasets are artificial, and real-world tasks will differ systematically, likely with systematic changes in detector performance.
future_direction: Conduct additional experiments to assess whether models trained on more tokens make anomaly detection harder.
Develop benchmarks more closely aligned with intended real-world tasks.
Advances in both detection and evaluation are needed for high-stakes settings.
papers.abstract: As LLMs grow in capability, the task of supervising LLMs becomes more challenging. Supervision failures can occur if LLMs are sensitive to factors that supervisors are unaware of. We investigate Mechanistic Anomaly Detection (MAD) as a technique to augment supervision of capable models; we use internal model features to identify anomalous training signals so they can be investigated or discarded. We train detectors to flag points from the test environment that differ substantially from the training environment, and experiment with a large variety of detector features and scoring rules to detect anomalies in a set of ``quirky'' language models. We find that detectors can achieve high discrimination on some tasks, but no detector is effective across all models and tasks. MAD techniques may be effective in low-stakes applications, but advances in both detection and evaluation are likely needed if they are to be used in high stakes settings.

papers.title: Beyond Activation Patterns: A Weight-Based Out-of-Context Explanation of Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we interpret Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features from a weight-based, out-of-context perspective to understand their computational roles, beyond activation patterns?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a weight-based, out-of-context interpretation framework for SAE features that reveals their computational roles in output prediction and attention mechanisms, complementing activation-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Weight-based, out-of-context analysis provides the missing half of SAE feature interpretability, revealing computational roles and depth-dependent functional specialization that activation patterns alone cannot capture.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 1/4 of SAE features directly predict output tokens when analyzed through their decoder-unembedding interactions.
Semantic features exhibit a U-shaped distribution across depth in Gemma models (high in early and late layers) and a monotonic distribution in Llama models, revealing architectural differences in functional specialization.
Features actively participate in attention mechanisms, with pre- and post-softmax analysis showing depth-dependent structure and distinct profiles for semantic vs. non-semantic populations.
Weight-based analysis uncovers that early-layer features in Llama specialize for input token recognition (encoder-embedding alignment) while late-layer features specialize for output prediction (decoder-unembedding alignment).
The out-of-context framework provides a complementary, causal perspective on feature function that activation-based methods miss.
papers.limitation:
The out-of-context framework is strict and simulates attention competition across the entire SAE dictionary, which may not reflect the contextual sparsity of actual forward passes and could underestimate feature importance.
The analysis focuses on intra-layer attention (features in layer L interacting with QK circuits in layer L+1) and may miss features specialized for longer-range, inter-layer interactions.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful technique for decomposing language model representations into interpretable features. Current interpretation methods infer feature semantics from activation patterns, but overlook that features are trained to reconstruct activations that serve computational roles in the forward pass. We introduce a novel weight-based interpretation framework that measures functional effects through direct weight interactions, requiring no activation data. Through three experiments on Gemma-2 and Llama-3.1 models, we demonstrate that (1) 1/4 of features directly predict output tokens, (2) features actively participate in attention mechanisms with depth-dependent structure, and (3) semantic and non-semantic feature populations exhibit distinct distribution profiles in attention circuits. Our analysis provides the missing out-of-context half of SAE feature interpretability.

papers.title: On the Theoretical Understanding of Identifiable Sparse Autoencoders and Beyond
papers.research_question: Can SAEs recover the ground truth monosemantic features from the polysemantic inputs?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a theoretical framework showing that standard Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) generally fail to fully recover ground-truth monosemantic features unless they are extremely sparse, and proposes a reweighted SAE (WSAE) that improves feature recovery by adaptively weighting dimensions based on their polysemantic level.
papers.conclusion: SAEs have inherent limits and cannot fully disentangle features under realistic sparsity; they should be regarded as an approximation tool. The proposed WSAE enhances feature recovery and interpretability in low-sparsity scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs generally fail to fully recover ground truth monosemantic features due to feature shrinking and feature vanishing.
SAEs can fully recover ground truth features only under the condition of extreme sparsity.
The proposed Weighted Sparse Autoencoder (WSAE) narrows the gap between polysemantic feature reconstruction and ground truth feature reconstruction, leading to better recovery.
Experiments on synthetic data validate the theoretical findings on sparsity and the improvement from reweighting.
Experiments on real language (Pythia, Llama) and vision (ResNet) models show that WSAE enhances feature monosemanticity and interpretability compared to standard SAEs.
papers.limitation: SAE-based interpretability should be regarded as an approximation tool, not as a faithful feature recovery mechanism, because full disentanglement is mathematically impossible under realistic sparsity.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for interpreting features learned by large language models (LLMs). It aims to recover complex superposed polysemantic features into interpretable monosemantic ones through feature reconstruction via sparsely activated neural networks. Despite the wide applications of SAEs, it remains unclear under what conditions an SAE can fully recover the ground truth monosemantic features from the superposed polysemantic ones. In this paper, through theoretical analysis, we for the first time propose the necessary and sufficient conditions for identifiable SAEs (SAEs that learn unique and ground truth monosemantic features), including 1) extreme sparsity of the ground truth feature, 2) sparse activation of SAEs, and 3) enough hidden dimensions of SAEs. Moreover, when the identifiable conditions are not fully met, we propose a reweighting strategy to improve the identifiability. Specifically, following the theoretically suggested weight selection principle, we prove that the gap between the loss functions of SAE reconstruction and monosemantic feature reconstruction can be narrowed, so that the reweighted SAEs have better reconstruction of the ground truth monosemantic features than the uniformly weighted ones. In experiments, we validate our theoretical findings and show that our weighted SAE significantly improves feature monosemanticity and interpretability.

papers.title: Decomposing The Dark Matter of Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What is the structure of SAE error (dark matter)? Can SAE error be predicted from activations? How do the linearly predictable and nonlinearly predictable components differ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that SAE error (dark matter) is largely linearly predictable from model activations, and that the nonlinear component is qualitatively different, containing fewer not-yet-learned features and being harder to learn.
papers.conclusion: The fact that SAE error can be predicted and analyzed is surprising, indicating SAE errors are worthy of analysis. The presence of constant nonlinear error at fixed sparsity suggests scaling SAEs may not be the only way to explain more of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SAE error norms and vectors can be linearly predicted from activations with high accuracy (R2 between 70-95% for norms, 15-72% for vectors).
The scaling behavior of SAE error norms is predictable across different SAE sizes; larger SAEs struggle to reconstruct the same contexts as smaller SAEs.
The nonlinear component of SAE error contains fewer not-yet-learned features, is harder to learn SAEs for, and contributes proportionally to cross entropy loss.
Inference time gradient pursuit reduces total FVU by 3-5% but leaves nonlinear error mostly unchanged.
Linear transformations from earlier layer SAE outputs can reduce nonlinear error and total SAE error.
future_direction: Explore alternative penalties besides sparsity or new ways to learn better dictionaries.
Incorporate low-rank dense side channels in SAE architecture.
Use small-scale trials to forecast SAE scaling behavior.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a promising technique for decomposing language model activations into interpretable linear features. However, current SAEs fall short of completely explaining model performance, resulting in "dark matter": unexplained variance in activations. This work investigates dark matter as an object of study in its own right. Surprisingly, we find that much of SAE dark matter -- about half of the error vector itself and >90% of its norm -- can be linearly predicted from the initial activation vector. Additionally, we find that the scaling behavior of SAE error norms at a per token level is remarkably predictable: larger SAEs mostly struggle to reconstruct the same contexts as smaller SAEs. We build on the linear representation hypothesis to propose models of activations that might lead to these observations. These insights imply that the part of the SAE error vector that cannot be linearly predicted ("nonlinear" error) might be fundamentally different from the linearly predictable component. To validate this hypothesis, we empirically analyze nonlinear SAE error and show that 1) it contains fewer not yet learned features, 2) SAEs trained on it are quantitatively worse, and 3) it is responsible for a proportional amount of the downstream increase in cross entropy loss when SAE activations are inserted into the model. Finally, we examine two methods to reduce nonlinear SAE error: inference time gradient pursuit, which leads to a very slight decrease in nonlinear error, and linear transformations from earlier layer SAE outputs, which leads to a larger reduction.

papers.title: Capacity Matters: a Proof-of-Concept for Transformer Memorization on Real-World Data
papers.research_question: How do model architecture (embedding size, layers, activation functions) and data configurations (size, complexity) influence the empirical memorization capacity of generative transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that embedding size is the primary determinant of learning speed and capacity for memorization, while additional layers provide limited benefits and may hinder performance on simpler datasets. Softmax activation demonstrates greater stability and capacity, and increasing data complexity (sequences vs triplets) improves final memorization.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that embedding size and activation function have more impact on memorization capacity than depth, and that larger datasets improve memorization but require longer training. Sequences outperform triplets but introduce fluctuations, highlighting the importance of dataset structure.
papers.key_findings:
Embedding size is the primary factor influencing learning speed and capacity, while adding more layers does not improve memorization and can slow training.
Softmax activation function consistently outperforms ReLU, GELU, and RReLU in terms of stability and capacity, especially in deeper models.
Larger datasets require longer warm-up periods but achieve higher final memorization capacity, with a threshold beyond which training slows significantly.
Sequence-based datasets (simulating graph traversal) achieve near-perfect memorization faster than triplet datasets, though with increased training fluctuations.
For simple datasets, increasing embedding size is more beneficial than adding depth, and shallow architectures with wider embeddings are recommended for edge deployment.
papers.limitation:
Misclassification patterns were not systematically analyzed; unlearned samples may be due to optimization bottlenecks or data-specific challenges.
Layer similarity or redundancy was not directly assessed; future probing and pruning studies could clarify each layer's role.
The sequence generation method, while reflecting ontology traversal, could be more explicitly aligned with clinical reasoning patterns.
Experiments under quantization or activation sparsity constraints were not conducted, which may affect architectural recommendations for edge applications.
future_direction: Test findings on longer sequences and larger datasets to confirm scalability.
Integrate sparse autoencoders or transcoders to distinguish memorization from generalization.
Conduct experiments under quantization or activation sparsity constraints for edge deployment.
papers.abstract: This paper studies how the model architecture and data configurations influence the empirical memorization capacity of generative transformers. The models are trained using synthetic text datasets derived from the Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine (SNOMED) knowledge graph: triplets, representing static connections, and sequences, simulating complex relation patterns. The results show that embedding size is the primary determinant of learning speed and capacity, while additional layers provide limited benefits and may hinder performance on simpler datasets. Activation functions play a crucial role, and Softmax demonstrates greater stability and capacity. Furthermore, increasing the complexity of the data set seems to improve the final memorization. These insights improve our understanding of transformer memory mechanisms and provide a framework for optimizing model design with structured real-world data.

papers.title: Dense SAE Latents Are Features, Not Bugs
papers.research_question: Are dense latents in sparse autoencoders (SAEs) undesirable training artifacts or do they reflect meaningful model representations?
papers.core_contribution: Dense SAE latents are not training artifacts but reflect meaningful, functional representations in the language model's residual stream, serving roles such as position tracking, context binding, and entropy regulation.
papers.conclusion: Dense SAE latents serve functional roles in language model computation and should not be dismissed as training noise.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating the dense-latent subspace in the residual stream prevents new dense latents from being learned in retrained SAEs, indicating dense features are intrinsic to the residual space.
Dense latents tend to form antipodal pairs that reconstruct specific directions in the residual stream.
A taxonomy of dense latents identifies classes including position tracking, context binding, entropy regulation, alphabet (letter-specific output), part-of-speech, and PCA reconstruction.
The function of dense latents shifts across layers: from structural (e.g., position) in early layers, to semantic (e.g., context binding) in middle layers, to output-oriented (e.g., alphabet) in late layers.
Nullspace-aligned dense latents are causally involved in entropy regulation via interaction with RMSNorm scaling.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a few models (Gemma 2 2B, GPT-2, LLaMA 3.2) and SAE architectures (JumpReLU, TopK).
future_direction: Explore the circuits involving dense subspaces, particularly context-binding latents.
Investigate whether dense latents are a general phenomenon across more models and SAE variants.
Challenge the assumption of globally monosemantic directions and further study context-dependent feature binding.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are designed to extract interpretable features from language models by enforcing a sparsity constraint. Ideally, training an SAE would yield latents that are both sparse and semantically meaningful. However, many SAE latents activate frequently (i.e., are \emph{dense}), raising concerns that they may be undesirable artifacts of the training procedure. In this work, we systematically investigate the geometry, function, and origin of dense latents and show that they are not only persistent but often reflect meaningful model representations. We first demonstrate that dense latents tend to form antipodal pairs that reconstruct specific directions in the residual stream, and that ablating their subspace suppresses the emergence of new dense features in retrained SAEs -- suggesting that high density features are an intrinsic property of the residual space. We then introduce a taxonomy of dense latents, identifying classes tied to position tracking, context binding, entropy regulation, letter-specific output signals, part-of-speech, and principal component reconstruction. Finally, we analyze how these features evolve across layers, revealing a shift from structural features in early layers, to semantic features in mid layers, and finally to output-oriented signals in the last layers of the model. Our findings indicate that dense latents serve functional roles in language model computation and should not be dismissed as training noise.

papers.title: How Diffusion Models Memorize
papers.research_question: How do diffusion models memorize training data? The paper investigates the underlying mechanism of memorization in diffusion models, focusing on why and how it occurs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that memorization in diffusion models is driven by overestimation of training samples during early denoising, caused by classifier-free guidance, which collapses latent diversity and locks denoising trajectories onto memorized images.
papers.conclusion: Memorization arises from overestimation of memorized data in early denoising, and recognizing this regime could lead to safer, less replicative generative systems.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization cannot be explained by overfitting alone; with classifier-free guidance, training loss is larger in early denoising under memorization.
Memorized prompts inject training images into noise predictions, steering denoising toward paired samples.
Classifier-free guidance leads to overestimation of the training image, which grows linearly with the guidance scale.
Overestimation collapses latent diversity and causes denoising trajectories to converge quickly to the memorized image.
Deviations from the theoretical denoising schedule (in terms of contributions of x and x_T) correlate strongly with memorization severity.
papers.abstract: Despite their success in image generation, diffusion models can memorize training data, raising serious privacy and copyright concerns. Although prior work has sought to characterize, detect, and mitigate memorization, the fundamental question of why and how it occurs remains unresolved. In this paper, we revisit the diffusion and denoising process and analyze latent space dynamics to address the question: "How do diffusion models memorize?" We show that memorization is driven by the overestimation of training samples during early denoising, which reduces diversity, collapses denoising trajectories, and accelerates convergence toward the memorized image. Specifically: (i) memorization cannot be explained by overfitting alone, as training loss is larger under memorization due to classifier-free guidance amplifying predictions and inducing overestimation; (ii) memorized prompts inject training images into noise predictions, forcing latent trajectories to converge and steering denoising toward their paired samples; and (iii) a decomposition of intermediate latents reveals how initial randomness is quickly suppressed and replaced by memorized content, with deviations from the theoretical denoising schedule correlating almost perfectly with memorization severity. Together, these results identify early overestimation as the central underlying mechanism of memorization in diffusion models.

papers.title: Sparse Semantic Dimension as a Generalization Certificate for LLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models (LLMs) generalize robustly despite having parameter counts that vastly exceed the number of training tokens? The paper investigates whether the effective capacity controlling generalization lies in the low-dimensional, sparse geometry of the model's internal representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that the effective complexity of LLMs is governed by the sparse, low-dimensional manifold of internal representations, and introduces the Sparse Semantic Dimension (SSD) to provide non-vacuous generalization bounds that scale with the active feature pool rather than the parameter count.
papers.conclusion: The Sparse Semantic Dimension (SSD) resolves the generalization paradox by shifting the complexity measure from parameter count to the active feature pool, providing a mathematical certificate for generalization and a safety monitor for OOD detection via feature density.
papers.key_findings:
The SSD-based generalization bound becomes non-vacuous at realistic sample sizes (e.g., N≈50,000) for GPT-2 Small and Gemma-2B, where parameter-counting bounds would be vacuous.
Larger models (Gemma-2B) require significantly fewer calibration samples to identify their active manifold than smaller models (GPT-2), suggesting they learn more compressible, distinct semantic structures.
Out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs trigger a measurable 'feature explosion' (a sharp spike in active features), which serves as a reliable, computationally cheap proxy for epistemic uncertainty and can function as a safety monitor.
The generalization guarantee depends on the specific semantic alignment of activated SAE features, not just statistical sparsity, as shown by an ablation where shuffling feature indices causes a catastrophic increase in reconstruction error.
The framework decomposes generalization into interpretable components: empirical risk, reconstruction error, pool mismatch, and a complexity penalty based on the active concept pool size.
future_direction: Investigate how the ratio of SSD to parameter count evolves for frontier-scale models (e.g., 70B+ parameters) and whether a 'sparsity saturation' point exists.
Investigate layer-wise generalization dynamics by using SAEs at different layers to determine which layers govern memorization versus generalization.
Extend the theoretical bounds to account for dynamic or context-dependent concept pools to provide tighter guarantees for models operating in rapidly shifting domains.
papers.abstract: Standard statistical learning theory predicts that Large Language Models (LLMs) should overfit because their parameter counts vastly exceed the number of training tokens. Yet, in practice, they generalize robustly. We propose that the effective capacity controlling generalization lies in the geometry of the model's internal representations: while the parameter space is high-dimensional, the activation states lie on a low-dimensional, sparse manifold. To formalize this, we introduce the Sparse Semantic Dimension (SSD), a complexity measure derived from the active feature vocabulary of a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) trained on the model's layers. Treating the LLM and SAE as frozen oracles, we utilize this framework to attribute the model's generalization capabilities to the sparsity of the dictionary rather than the total parameter count. Empirically, we validate this framework on GPT-2 Small and Gemma-2B, demonstrating that our bound provides non-vacuous certificates at realistic sample sizes. Crucially, we uncover a counter-intuitive "feature sharpness" scaling law: despite being an order of magnitude larger, Gemma-2B requires significantly fewer calibration samples to identify its active manifold compared to GPT-2, suggesting that larger models learn more compressible, distinct semantic structures. Finally, we show that this framework functions as a reliable safety monitor: out-of-distribution inputs trigger a measurable "feature explosion" (a sharp spike in active features), effectively signaling epistemic uncertainty through learned feature violation. Code is available at: https://github.com/newcodevelop/sparse-semantic-dimension.

papers.title: Captured by Captions: On Memorization and its Mitigation in CLIP Models
papers.research_question: How does memorization manifest in multi-modal models like CLIP, which combine elements of supervised and self-supervised learning, and how can it be measured and mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes CLIPMem, a formal metric to measure memorization in CLIP models, and shows that memorization can be reduced while simultaneously improving model generalization, contrary to trends in supervised and self-supervised learning.
papers.conclusion: CLIPMem effectively quantifies memorization in CLIP, revealing that memorization is highest for mis-captioned and atypical samples and is more prominent in the text encoder; mitigation strategies can reduce memorization and improve generalization.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP's memorization behavior falls between that of supervised and self-supervised learning paradigms.
"Mis-captioned" (incorrect or imprecise) and atypical data points exhibit the highest levels of memorization.
The text encoder contributes more to memorization than the image encoder.
Mitigation strategies like text augmentations and noising text embeddings can reduce memorization while improving downstream generalization.
Removing highly memorized samples (especially mis-captioned ones) from training can improve model performance.
papers.abstract: Multi-modal models, such as CLIP, have demonstrated strong performance in aligning visual and textual representations, excelling in tasks like image retrieval and zero-shot classification. Despite this success, the mechanisms by which these models utilize training data, particularly the role of memorization, remain unclear. In uni-modal models, both supervised and self-supervised, memorization has been shown to be essential for generalization. However, it is not well understood how these findings would apply to CLIP, which incorporates elements from both supervised learning via captions that provide a supervisory signal similar to labels, and from self-supervised learning via the contrastive objective. To bridge this gap in understanding, we propose a formal definition of memorization in CLIP (CLIPMem) and use it to quantify memorization in CLIP models. Our results indicate that CLIP's memorization behavior falls between the supervised and self-supervised paradigms, with "mis-captioned" samples exhibiting highest levels of memorization. Additionally, we find that the text encoder contributes more to memorization than the image encoder, suggesting that mitigation strategies should focus on the text domain. Building on these insights, we propose multiple strategies to reduce memorization while at the same time improving utility--something that had not been shown before for traditional learning paradigms where reducing memorization typically results in utility decrease.

papers.title: Sparse but Wrong: Incorrect L0 Leads to Incorrect Features in Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How does the L0 hyperparameter (average number of active features per token) in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) affect the quality of learned features, and how can the correct L0 be determined?
papers.core_contribution: The L0 hyperparameter in Sparse Autoencoders must be set correctly to learn monosemantic features; if L0 is too low or too high, the SAE mixes correlated features, and the paper provides a proxy metric (decoder pairwise cosine similarity) to guide L0 selection.
papers.conclusion: The L0 hyperparameter must be set correctly for SAEs to learn correct, monosemantic features, and most existing SAEs likely have an L0 that is too low.
papers.key_findings:
If L0 is set too low, SAEs mix positively correlated features to improve reconstruction, leading to polysemantic latents.
If L0 is set too high, SAEs find degenerate solutions that also mix features.
Commonly used sparsity–reconstruction tradeoff plots are not a sound evaluation method, as they can favor incorrect SAEs that mix features over a ground-truth SAE.
A proxy metric, decoder pairwise cosine similarity (c_dec), is minimized when the SAE L0 matches the true underlying L0 of the data distribution.
Most commonly used open-source SAEs have an L0 that is too low.
papers.limitation:
The investigation is limited to features satisfying the linear representation hypothesis and does not consider non-linear underlying features.
The study only investigated a few layers of popular LLMs due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Investigate how SAEs react if the underlying features are non-linear.
Explore the impact of different correlation structures (e.g., unbalanced correlations) on SAEs.
Extend the analysis to more layers of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) extract features from LLM internal activations, meant to correspond to interpretable concepts. A core SAE training hyperparameter is L0: how many SAE features should fire per token on average. Existing work compares SAE algorithms using sparsity-reconstruction tradeoff plots, implying L0 is a free parameter with no single correct value aside from its effect on reconstruction. In this work we study the effect of L0 on SAEs, and show that if L0 is not set correctly, the SAE fails to disentangle the underlying features of the LLM. If L0 is too low, the SAE will mix correlated features to improve reconstruction. If L0 is too high, the SAE finds degenerate solutions that also mix features. Further, we present a proxy metric that can help guide the search for the correct L0 for an SAE on a given training distribution. We show that our method finds the correct L0 in toy models and coincides with peak sparse probing performance in LLM SAEs. We find that most commonly used SAEs have an L0 that is too low. Our work shows that L0 must be set correctly to train SAEs with correct features.

papers.title: Insights Into the Inner Workings of Transformer Models for Protein Function Prediction
papers.research_question: How can explainable AI methods be extended to inspect latent representations in transformer models for protein function prediction, and do the identified relevant sequence parts reflect biological expectations?
papers.core_contribution: Extends integrated gradients to compute head-specific attributions in transformers for protein function prediction, showing that attribution maps correlate with biological sequence annotations and identifying specialized heads.
papers.conclusion: The extended integrated gradients method provides insights into transformer models for protein function prediction, showing that models focus on biologically relevant sequence parts and that specific heads are specialized for certain annotations.
papers.key_findings:
Attribution maps at the embedding layer correlate significantly with UniProt annotations for EC classes and GO membrane term.
Inside the model, specific transformer heads show significant correlation between attributions and annotations, indicating specialization.
For GO membrane term, heads with positive relevance and correlation with transmembrane regions are identified.
For GO catalytic activity, heads correlate with active sites and PROSITE patterns.
The method is sensitive to model parameters and provides insights beyond anecdotal evidence.
papers.limitation: The method may identify significant heads due to coincidental partial alignment of randomly initialized heads with directions in feature space that happen to correlate with sequence annotations.
papers.abstract: Motivation: We explored how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) can help to shed light into the inner workings of neural networks for protein function prediction, by extending the widely used XAI method of integrated gradients such that latent representations inside of transformer models, which were finetuned to Gene Ontology term and Enzyme Commission number prediction, can be inspected too. Results: The approach enabled us to identify amino acids in the sequences that the transformers pay particular attention to, and to show that these relevant sequence parts reflect expectations from biology and chemistry, both in the embedding layer and inside of the model, where we identified transformer heads with a statistically significant correspondence of attribution maps with ground truth sequence annotations (e.g. transmembrane regions, active sites) across many proteins. Availability and Implementation: Source code can be accessed at https://github.com/markuswenzel/xai-proteins .

papers.title: DGTN: Graph-Enhanced Transformer with Diffusive Attention Gating Mechanism for Enzyme DDG Prediction
papers.research_question: How can we accurately predict the effect of amino acid mutations on enzyme thermodynamic stability (∆∆G) by integrating sequence and structural information through a co-learning framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DGTN, a novel architecture that co-learns graph neural network and transformer representations through a bidirectional diffusion mechanism for protein stability prediction, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
papers.conclusion: DGTN effectively integrates 3D geometric and evolutionary sequence context through bidirectional diffusion, establishing a principled and interpretable paradigm for accurate protein stability prediction and design.
papers.key_findings:
DGTN achieves state-of-the-art performance on ProTherm with Pearson correlation ρ=0.87 and RMSE=1.21 kcal/mol, outperforming existing baselines.
Ablation studies show the bidirectional diffusion mechanism contributes a 6-point gain in Pearson correlation over simple cross-modal fusion.
The model generalizes well to unseen datasets (SKEMPI, Ssym, FireProtDB), demonstrating robust learning of stability principles.
Theoretical analysis proves the diffused attention converges to an optimal structure-aware attention matrix with a convergence rate of O(1/√T).
Attention visualization confirms the model successfully identifies spatially proximate but sequentially distant residue interactions.
papers.limitation:
Operates on a single static conformation of the wild-type protein, unable to capture dynamic or entropic contributions to stability.
Evaluates mutations in isolation and does not explicitly model epistatic (non-additive) interactions between multiple substitutions.
Training data (ProTherm) exhibits class imbalance, with certain protein families overrepresented, potentially limiting generalization.
